newsitem.title: UK: British manufacturing recovers slowly in November.
newsitem.headline: British manufacturing recovers slowly in November.

text.p: Britain's manufacturing sector grew for the sixth month in a row in November but the pace of recovery remained sluggish, a leading business group said on Monday.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said overall the manufacturing economy expanded but there was a slight slackening in the pace of growth which could take some pressure off the government to raise interest rates again soon.
Its purchasing managers' index (PMI) fell to a seasonally- adjusted 54.4 percent from 54.5 percent in October. A reading over 50 indicates the manufacturing sector is growing.
Strong growth in output and new orders were behind the latest expansion, the CIPS said.
"The improvement in order books occurred in spite of the recent rise in the sterling exchange rate."
Export orders grew in November, but the CIPS said the strong pound has dented activity in parts of the manufacturing sector, which is heavily dependent on overseas markets.
The pound has rallied dramatically since the summer, appreciating by around 10 percent between August and November on a trade-weighted basis.
"The stronger pound was reported to have dampened demand for certain goods," the CIPS said. "However, greater demand for goods in the domestic market made up for any export lossses."

City economists said sterling's appreciation was a severe setback to the manufacturing sector which has only recently shown tentative signs of recovery and still lags the lively activity seen in other areas of the economy.

"The message from the survey is that we are seeing a very slow recovery in the manufacturing sector and it is clear stronger sterling is going to have an impact on demand," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.
But the November survey may help Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke resist any call for higher interest rates from the Bank of England at their monthly meeting next week.
Clarke will meet central bank governor Eddie George to discuss the level of rates on December 11 when most analysts expect George to call for another rise in the 6.0 percent base rate.
However, a poll conducted by Reuters after the November 26 budget showed most economists expected Clarke to delay any rate rise until next year.

"Clarke presented the budget as a tight fiscal package designed to prevent interest rates going up aggressively, so if he raises rates next week he will be admitting to a certain amount of failure," said Cates.
Clarke made a small income tax cut in the budget, but this was more than offset by planned cuts in public spending.
The CIPS' findings on manufacturing prices should also help Clarke to fend off calls for higher rates.
The survey showed input prices fell for the thirteenth month in a row in November and by a greater extent than in October.
"The recent increase in deflationary pressures was almost entirely a result of the stronger pound making imported inputs cheaper in sterling terms," CIPS said.

Underlying inflation accelerated to 3.3 percent in the year to October, well above the government's 2.5 percent target, but Clarke may argue that the lower commodity prices reported by the CIPS have yet to fully feed though to retail prices.
The Bank of England released data on Monday showing rapid growth of narrow money supply continued unabated in November.

M0, which chiefly covers notes and coins in curculation, grew a seasonally-adjusted 7.5 percent in the year to November. That was unchanged from October's growth rate but still well above the government's zero to four percent monitoring range.
"This points tentatively to a slight rise in the level of high street activity in November," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Accelerating M0 suggests growth in consumer spending and the indicator has a good record in signalling higher inflation in the future.
